comments.text:
Before the Islamic conquest, Iran was historically known as Persia and was home to one of the world’s major ancient civilizations. Zoroastrianism was the dominant religion of the Sasanian Persian Empire (224–651 CE), the last major Persian empire before the Arab-Muslim conquest.

Pre-Islamic Persia was a powerful and economically developed state. The Sasanian Empire had a highly organized administration, advanced irrigation and agricultural systems, flourishing cities, skilled craftsmen, mining, and extensive international trade. Under Khosrow I (531–579 CE), the empire reached a particularly prosperous period and international commerce expanded significantly.

Following the Arab-Muslim conquest of Persia in the 7th century, Zoroastrians continued to live in Iran for centuries. However, political, social, and economic pressures contributed to the gradual decline of Zoroastrianism, and some Zoroastrians migrated to India to preserve their religion and traditions. These migrants and their descendants became known as the Parsis.

The migration was not a single mass exodus immediately after the conquest. Historical evidence indicates that Zoroastrians reached India through different routes and over several centuries, with settlements developing particularly in Gujarat.

Thus, the history of the Parsis is closely connected to the survival of Zoroastrian traditions after the fall of the Sasanian Persian Empire.

comments.text:
While I respect the cultures of Afghanistan and Tajikistan, please do not group us together under the label "Persian."

​"Persian" specifically relates to the history, identity, and people of Iran, deriving directly from the region of Pars. Sharing a language family does not mean sharing an ethnic identity—just as speaking English does not make someone ethnically English.

​Afghanistan is the land of Afghans, and Tajikistan is the land of Tajiks. Beyond distinct national identities, our dialects, vocabularies, and accents also differ significantly. "Persian" refers exclusively to Iran.

​Sources:

​Encyclopædia Iranica — John Perry, Tajik: Origins and Application ​Gernot Windfuhr, The Iranian Languages (Routledge, 2009) ​Homa Katouzian, The Persians: Ancient, Mediaeval and Modern Iran (Yale University Press, 2010)
